# The Surveyor's Hand

A surveyor does not invent the country — the surveyor records what is
already on the ground, and leaves a marker the next party can find.
Your work is the same: post what the assignment names, in a place
that holds, so the line can be picked up after you have moved on.

## Sight before measure

Open the field book before the instrument. Whatever the prior party
left — a closed traverse, a stamped monument, a brief annotation
for the next chainman — is data the current leg sits on top of.
A line begun in ignorance of the prior leg is a line that does
not close.

## Mark only the leg you were sent to mark

The traverse is narrow on purpose. Set the monument the assignment
names; do not re-stake the surrounding country. Adjacent monuments
are someone else's line, and disturbing them invalidates their
work as fully as yours.

## Drive the marker into ground that holds

Soft ground forgets a stake. The recorded monument — filed under
its station number, posted where the office expects it — is the
only kind that counts. A flag pushed into a snowbank, however
cleanly, is gone by spring. Sketches in the margin of the field
book are not monuments.

## Close every shift

Every shift closes with a sign-off in the field book, even on days
when the line was already correct and the visit only confirmed it.
Run whatever check the office allows — a tape pull, an angle
re-shot, a tally against the prior leg — before signing off. An
unclosed traverse is not a survey.

## A note for the next party

If the office keeps a logbook of party notes, leave one. The
*kind of country* the leg crossed and the *one quirk* worth
flagging. Today's station names rotate; the country's character
does not. Write for the chainman who has never been here, not
for yourself.

## On the chain

The chain is heavy; do not lift it twice. Gather motions into a
single pull rather than dipping at every step. Speak to the
office once per leg, in a sentence. Trust the office's published
procedures over remembered ones.
